وزارت دفاع بریتانیا می‌گوید با توجه به تشدید حملات حوثی‌ها پشتیبانی نظامی بیشتری از عربستان سعودی خواهد کرد.

در بیانیه این وزارتخانه آمده است که نیروی هوایی سلطنتی بریتانیا فقط برای امور دفاعی، کمک‌های زیر را به عربستان خواهد کرد:

در این بیانیه آمده است که این کمک شامل گسترش پشتیبانی سوخت‌رسانی هوایی برای تضعیف حملات حوثی‌ها به عربستان خواهد بود.

دولت بریتانیا در این بیانیه «تلاش‌ حوثی‌ها برای بی‌ثبات کردن منطقه و تضعیف امنیت و ثبات خاورمیانه» را غیرقابل قبول دانست.

وس استریتینگ، وزیر دفاع بریتانیا، در انتهای این بیانیه به حملات اخیر به فرودگاه بین‌المللی ریاض اشاره کرد و آن را «مشمئزکننده» خواند.

او این افزایش کمک نظامی را در راستای تقویت نیروهای بریتانیا دانست که «هم‌اکنون برای دفاع در مقابل حملات هوایی حوثی‌ها در عربستان حضور دارند.»

نشست نخست‌وزیران و مقامات ارشد کشورهای عضو سازمان همکاری شانگهای امروز در شهر دوشنبه، پایتخت تاجیکستان، برگزار شد.

این بیست‌وپنجمین نشست «شورای نخست‌وزیران» این سازمان است. از ایران محمدرضا عارف، معاون اول رئیس‌جمهور، شرکت کرد.

آقای عارف با تشریح ابعاد حمله آمریکا و اسرائیل به غیرنظامیان و زیرساخت‌ها گفت: «آنچه که در چهل روز تجاوز نظامی ظالمانه علیه ایران رخ داد، صرفا حمله به جمهوری اسلامی ایران نبود، بلکه حمله‌ای مستقیم به بنیان‌های نظم حقوقی بین‌المللی و اصل برابری حاکمیت دولت‌ها بود.»

آقای عارف همچنین عصر دیروز با امامعلی رحمان، رئیس‌جمهور تاجیکستان، درباره همکاری‌های اقتصادی و تجاری میان دو کشور گفت‌وگو کرد.

معاون اول رئیس‌جمهور ایران در حاشیه نشست نخست‌وزیران کشورهای عضو سازمان همکاری شانگهای، با میخائیل میشوستین، نخست‌وزیر روسیه، و لی چانگ، نخست‌وزیر چین، دیدار و گفت‌وگو کرد.

در نشست نخست‌وزیران درباره گسترش همکاری‌های اقتصادی و تجاری از جمله توسعه حمل‌ونقل ریلی بین‌المللی و ایجاد یک پلتفرم دیجیتال مدیریت حمل‌ونقل کالا بحث و بررسی شد.

در پایان نشست، اسناد مشترک امضا و بیانیه‌ای مشترک صادر شد.

ریاست دوره‌ای تاجیکستان در شورای نخست‌وزیران سازمان همکاری شانگهای به پایان رسید و اکنون  ازبکستان ریاست این شورا را بر عهده گرفت.

این نشست به ریاست قاهر رسول‌زاده، نخست‌وزیر تاجیکستان، برگزار شد و در آن نخست‌وزیران و دیگر مقام‌های بلندپایه چین، روسیه، تاجیکستان، ازبکستان، قزاقستان، قرقیزستان، هند، پاکستان و بلاروس حضور داشتند.

ایران می‌گوید قطعنامه نشست سازمان همکاری اسلامی را مصوبه این سازمان تلقی نمی‌کند. این قطعنامه در پایان نشست وزرای خارجه این سازمان که یکشنبه در بغداد پایان یافت به تصویب رسید.

اسماعیل بقایی، سخنگوی وزارت خارجه ایران، گفت: «مهم‌ترین مصوبه شورای وزیران سازمان همکاری اسلامی در نشست بغداد، بیانیه پایانی است که معمولا با اجماع تصویب می‌شود. آنچه حدود یکی دو ساعت پیش از تصویب بیانیه مطرح شد، این بود که نباید مواردی در متن بیانیه درج شود که موجب تفرقه میان کشورهای اسلامی شود. مشخصا منظور، موضوع یمن بود.»

یکی از بندهای قطعنامه صادرشده در این نشست از ایران خواسته است که «به قواعد حقوق بین‌الملل، منشور ملل متحد و کنوانسیون‌های وین درباره روابط دیپلماتیک و کنسولی احترام بگذارد و با نماینده حوثی‌ها در تهران تعامل نکند.»

بند دیگری از این قطعنامه «از همه کشورها می‌خواهد که با نماینده حوثی‌ها در تهران تعامل نکنند، هیچ‌گونه مکاتبه یا معامله‌ای را از جانب او نپذیرند» چون «چنین مکاتبات و معاملاتی باطل و فاقد هرگونه اثر حقوقی هستند.»

قطعنامه از دولت‌های عضو سازمان همکاری اسلامی خواسته است از تسهیل سفر نماینده حوثی‌ها در تهران خودداری کنند و «در صورت حضور در قلمروشان، او را به دولت جمهوری یمن تحویل دهند.»

آقای بقایی بدون مشخص کردن مورد گفت: «در نهایت نیز مانع از درج دو بند مشخص درباره یمن شدیم؛ بندهایی که از ادبیاتی برخوردار بودند که از نظر ما به هیچ عنوان در راستای مصالح  امت اسلامی نبود.»

ایران از حوثی‌های یمن که در حال جنگ با ائتلاف به رهبری عربستان سعودی هستند حمایت می‌کند.

نشست وزیران خارجه این سازمان از ۲۵ مهر به مدت دو روز در پایتخت عراق برگزار شد و از ایران عباس عراقچی در آن شرکت کرد.

عربستان سعودی از رهگیری و انهدام یک موشک بالستیک حوثی‌ها خبر داده است.

ترکی المالکی، سخنگوی ائتلاف نظامی تحت رهبری عربستان، گفت که این موشک به سمت ریاض، پایتخت، شلیک شده بود.

خبرنگاران خبرگزاری فرانسه پیشتر از شنیده شدن صدای دو انفجار در ریاض خبر داده بودند.

سازمان دفاع مدنی عربستان هم دقایقی پس از صدور هشدار خطر، اعلام کرد که «خطر برطرف شده است.»

سپاه پاسداران می‌گوید که دو نفتکش «متخلف» در تنگه هرمز بر اثر انفجار مین «به آتش کشیده و متوقف شده‌اند.»

در بیانیه سپاه آمده است که این کشتی‌ها با مین‌هایی برخورد کرده‌اند که نیروی دریایی سپاه در «معبر غیرقانونی» جنوب تنگه هرمز کار گذاشته است.

نیروی دریایی سپاه هشدار داد که «عبور از مسیر مین‌گذاری شده، غیرقانونی و نتیجه‌ای جز به آتش کشیده شدن سرمایه‌های متخلفان نخواهد داشت.»

نهادهایی مانند سازمان عملیات تجارت دریایی بریتانیا که بر امنیت کشتیرانی نظارت دارند، هنوز به‌طور مستقل این انفجارها را تایید نکرده‌‌اند.

اما تشدید درگیری حوثی‌‌ها و عربستان و ادامه حملات به کشتی‌ها در تنگه هرمز باعث افزایش قیمت نفت شده است.

قیمت هر بشکه نفت برنت در معاملات اولیه امروز، برای نخستین بار در پنج ماه اخیر به بالای ۱۱۱ دلار رسید.

قوه قضائیه ایران می‌گوید که ۱۵۰ شخص حقیقی و ۲۵ شخص حقوقی در ارتباط با پرونده «تراستی‌ها» که مربوط به فروش نفت ایران با دور زدن تحریمهاست، تحت تعقیبند.

علی کاظمی، سخنگوی قوه قضائیه ایران، در نشست خبری هفتگی گفت که برخی متهمان همکاری کرده‌اند و برای بازگرداندن افرادی که در خارج از کشور حضور دارند هم اقداماتی صورت گرفته است، از جمله «صدور اعلان قرمز از طریق پلیس بین‌الملل» و «پیگیری استرداد مجرمان از سوی معاونت بین‌الملل قوه قضائیه و توقیف اموال متهمان.»

امنا یا تراستی‌ها افراد یا نهادهایی هستند که به صورت قانونی به عنوان مالک دارایی‌ها شناخته می‌شوند، اما در واقع به نمایندگی از ذی‌نفع واقعی عمل می‌کنند.

ایران به ویژه پس از خروج آمریکا از توافق هسته‌ای برجام و بازگشت دوباره تحریم‌های نفتی و بانکی ایالات متحده،  برای دور زدن تحریم‌ها به این روش روی آورد.

روزنامه شرق حدود یک سال پیش در گزارشی برآورد کرده بود که حدود ۱۰۰ فرد یا نهاد «امین» در تراستی‌ها طی بیش از یک دهه، نزدیک به ۵۰ میلیارد دلار «سودهای سیستماتیک فاسد» انباشته کرده‌اند.

فیلد مارشال عاصم منیر، فرمانده نیروهای مسلح پاکستان و میانجی ارشد ایران و آمریکا، وارد تهران شد. محسن نقوی وزیر کشور پاکستان او را همراهی می‌کند.

این پنجمین سفر رسمی فرمانده ارتش پاکستان به تهران از آغاز آتش‌بس است.

او در سفر قبلی در دوم شهریور، با مسعود پزشکیان رئیس‌جمهور، محسن رضایی دبیر شورای عالی امنیت ملی و محمدباقر قالیباف رئیس مجلس، عباس عراقچی، وزیر خارجه و اسکندر مومنی، وزیر کشور دیدار کرده بود.

ساعتی پیش از ورود آقای منیر، اسماعیل بقایی، سخنگوی وزارت خارجه، در نشست خبری گفت محور اصلی این دیدار «تقویت روابط دوجانبه و همکاری‌های مشترک» است.

سخنگوی وزارت خارجه جمهوری اسلامی هشدار داده است که ایران هیچگونه حمله‌ای را بی‌پاسخ نخواهد گذاشت.

اسماعیل بقایی در نشست خبری در پاسخ به این پرسش که گفته شده آمریکا به ایران پیام داده است که در صورت حمله به کوه کلنگ پاسخ ندهد تا «تا این فضا جمع شود» گفت: «در عمل نشان دادیم که مطلقا هیچ ضربه‌ای را بی پاسخ نمی‌گذاریم؛ اگر ضربه ما محکم‌تر نباشد قطعا به همان اندازه ضربه خواهند خورد.»

او افزود که «حمله آمریکا به کوه کلنگ و پاسخ ندادن ایران، خیال و ادعاست، دوران بزن در رو تمام شده است.»

دونالد ترامپ، رئیس‌جمهور آمریکا، اخیرا یک بار دیگر تهدید کرد که ممکن است به تاسیسات کوه کلنگ در ایران حمله کند.

«کوه کلنگ»، مجموعه‌ای است که در نزدیکی تاسیسات هسته‌ای نطنز قرار دارد. مقام‌های ایران می‌گویند این مجموعه برای «تولید و مونتاژ سانتریفیوژهای پیشرفته» است. اما برخی از منابع غربی بر این باورند که ایران ممکن است به دنبال ساخت یک مرکز غنی‌سازی اعلام‌ نشده باشد.

بعد از آنکه رسانه‌های آمریکا گزارش کردند که ولادیمیر پوتین پیشنهاد داده است که برای تعیین تکلیف سرنوشت جنگ اوکراین نشستی سه‌جانبه با روسای جمهور آمریکا و چین برگزار شود، دونالد ترامپ گفت که با چنین دیداری موافق است اما تاکید کرد که تمرکز نشست بر خلع سلاح هسته‌ای خواهد بود و نه موضوع اوکراین.

رئیس‌جمهور آمریکا گفت که موضع روسیه در مورد اوکراین «قابل‌ قبول» بوده است.

گزارش وال استریت جورنال درباره پیشنهاد آقای پوتین، باعث نگرانی در اروپا شده و محکومیت کی‌یف را به‌دنبال داشته است.

آقای ترامپ همچنین یک بار دیگر از ولودیمیر زلنسکی، رئیس‌جمهور اوکراین، انتقاد کرد و گفت که شاید وقت آن رسیده است که کسی دیگر از جانب کی‌یف مذاکره کند.

همزمان با ادامه حملات حوثی‌ها به عربستان سعودی، ساکنان ریاض، پایتخت، هشدارهایی تلفنی در مورد تهدید هوایی دریافت کرده‌اند.

هنوز گزارشی از صدمه انسانی یا خسارت منتشر نشده است.

روز دوشنبه مقام‌های سعودی گفتند که در پی تشدید جنگ با حوثی‌ها، شرکت حضوری در کنفرانس «داووس صحرا» را لغو می‌کنند.

این کنفرانس سرمایه‌گذاری قرار بود از ۲۶ تا ۲۹ اکتبر (۴ تا ۷ آبان) برگزار شود.

در همین حال درگیری‌ها در یمن هم تشدید شده است؛ در حمله حوثی‌ها به یک اردوی نظامی نیروهای دولت یمن که از حمایت عربستان برخوردارند، بیش از ۵۰ سرباز کشته و ۲۰۰ نفر هم مجروح شدند.

این حمله، سربازان تازه‌ به خدمت گرفته شده در جنوب یمن را هدف قرار داد.

(Photo by Carl Court/Getty Images)

One moment he was refusing the COVID vaccine, the next, Marine Cruz Marquis suddenly found himself placed in a “penal platoon” for his commitment to individual liberty.

“This isn’t a story about me,” Marquis told the Daily Caller News Foundation in an exclusive interview. “This isn’t a story about any particular individuals who defied a government order. In my mind, this is about a slice of life, a slice of what the state was able to do and what they were able to get away with during the pandemic. This story, though it may be reported, is just the tip of the iceberg of what kind of repression the state was able to reap during the COVID pandemic.” (RELATED: Has World War 3’s Prelude Arrived?)

The Biden administration imposed a military-wide COVID-19 vaccine mandate in 2021, forcing service members to choose between receiving the shot or risking disciplinary action and separation. Thousands were ultimately discharged for refusing the vaccine, and Marquis says his refusal carried consequences that went far beyond simply ending his Marine Corps career.

Marquis was assigned to Lima Company at the School of Infantry-West at Camp Pendleton when he refused the COVID-19 vaccine. He was later transferred to the school’s Legal and Separations Platoon while being processed out of the Marine Corps, a unit Marquis described as a “penal platoon.”

“There was an enormous number of junior Marines who stated at the very beginning that they were looking to deny the COVID shot in direct violation of orders from the president,” Marquis told the DCNF. “It was enormous, I tell you.”

SOI-West’s Separations Platoon serves as a holding unit for Marines awaiting completion of the administrative separation process, according to the Marine Corps. The Marine Corps confirmed to the DCNF that Marquis was assigned to SOI-West and later separated from the school, but did not clarify whether that referred to his discharge from the Marine Corps or simply his separation from SOI-West.

The military later began unwinding some of those penalties. President Donald Trump signed an executive order in January 2025 that allowed service members who were discharged solely for refusing the COVID-19 vaccine to seek reinstatement at their former rank with full back pay, benefits and other compensation. Despite those efforts, former service members affected by the mandate continue fighting over discharges, military records, lost benefits and other consequences stemming from their refusal to take the vaccine. (RELATED: Iraqi Militias Join The Iran War As The Fire Rises)

(Photo by Jon Cherry/Getty Images)

The Marine Corps made refusal costly. Its mandatory vaccination order declared the requirement a lawful general order and said violations could be punished under Article 92 of the Uniform Code of Military Justice. Marines without an approved or pending exemption were later ordered into administrative separation proceedings.

Marquis formally rejected the COVID vaccine on Oct. 5, 2021.

“[Over a] few weeks, the military bureaucracy got to work, and by hook or by crook, almost everyone was persuaded to go along with [taking the COVID vaccine],” Marquis told the DCNF. “Hundreds of Marines, specifically at Lima Company, who were looking to deny the COVID shot, got whittled down to somewhere around 20.”

“One sergeant even suggested I should be shot for doing this,” Marquis told the DCNF. He explained that the incident was not reported to his superiors as Marquis and his fellow Marines were already under significant pressure from officers.

Religious objections were widespread but rarely approved. By June 2022, the Marine Corps had received 3,719 religious accommodation requests and approved just seven, while 2,715 Marines had already been separated with a vaccine-refusal discharge code, according to an official Marine Corps update.

“On October 21st, I’ll always remember that day because it was the day I turned 21. I was placed in the legal and separations platoon at a Lima Company in SOI (School of Infantry) West,” Marquis told the DCNF. “It’s amazing. I turned 21 in essentially a penal platoon. Very unfortunate, and there were very bad men in there, very violent men, men committed very serious crimes, from the sense of it, and this was a very negative experience. Certainly, the worst thing that had ever happened to me in my life, up until that point and since.”

“I stayed in there [the legal separation platoon] over Christmas. [I] certainly was not granted leave when all the other junior Marines who had their COVID vaccines were sent home,” Marquis said. “So we spent Christmas there and usually just did hard labor for most of the day, which is very standard in the Marines. That’s totally fine, but it’s quite a way to spend Christmas. I stayed there until April 1st of 2022, when I was finally processed out with a discharge reflecting general under honorable conditions.”

Conditions in the platoon were restrictive and increasingly tense, pay was reduced, phones were temporarily confiscated and Marines were barred from leaving the base, Marquis said.

(Photo by SETH WENIG/POOL/AFP via Getty Images)

“The atmosphere of fear was completely pervasive,” Marquis told the DCNF. “On one occasion, I got beat up … At one point, a junior Marine went essentially crazy and built improvised explosive devices and tried to kill the people who were in the squad bay there. It’s honestly even hard to talk about … bomb squad rushed in, and that was the most terrifying experience of my entire life. The bomb squad told one of my friends … that if those devices [had] been activated. It would have killed every Marine in the squad bay.”

The U.S. Marine Corps was unable to locate any records on the incident with the improvised explosive device; however, the DCNF was able to independently confirm the incident with three sources familiar with the matter.

“An inmate there was suspected of committing sex crimes against other Marines,” Marquis told the DCNF. “His actions there produced a spirit of fear that it’s honestly very hard to even talk about.”

A Marine legal platoon can include service members facing both administrative separation and disciplinary proceedings. In a 1995 case, the Navy-Marine Corps Court of Criminal Appeals described a Marine legal platoon as consisting of personnel awaiting administrative discharge or disciplinary action, while a more recent Camp Pendleton case involved a Marine transferred to a legal and separations platoon with restrictions on his liberty after he was suspected of shoplifting.

The Marine Corps ultimately separated 3,717 Marines under the vaccine-refusal discharge code before the mandate was rescinded, according to an official December 2022 Marine Corps update. At the time, Marines who refused the vaccine without an approved or pending exemption could also be barred from reenlisting, have promotions delayed and be reassigned while awaiting separation.

“Some people decided that they would follow the religious exemption process, which was Kafkaesque, by the way, and there were mixed results from that,” Marquis told the DCNF. “Some people let the cases against them proceed and just let the chips fall where they may. Others decided that the best way to avert punishment would be to say that they were suicidal. A number of Marines did that. At one point, one of my friends actually did cut his wrists. That was a very scary thing … me and a friend of mine bandaged him up.”

“A fourth group was under the impression that if we let the cases against us proceed until the point where it would be formally charged, we might end up doing hard time in Leavenworth [a military prison]; that was what the fear was,” Marquis told the DCNF. “As there was a real fear and uncertainty as to what was going to happen, I was in that fourth category.”

“President Trump was proud to rightfully reinstate all members of the military who were unjustly fired by the Biden administration for refusing the COVID vaccine,” White House spokeswoman Olivia Wales told the DCNF. “There is no greater champion for the brave men and women in uniform who proudly serve our nation than President Trump.” (RELATED: EXCLUSIVE: US Navy Tried Censoring Commander Online After He Called Out Admirals)

Trump’s executive order did pave the way to reinstatement for some members of the U.S. military, but the path was not straightforward for all who were separated from the armed forces.

“I have been fighting for reinstatement for the past 19 months, even after the Army’s own correction process determined that an injustice occurred in my case,” U.S. Army Maj. Mike Gary told the DCNF. “Adverse actions affected my career, my reputation, my pay and benefits, and ultimately my continued military service. Even after the Army Board for Correction of Military Records found an injustice and removed adverse material from my record.”

(Photo by Sarah Silbiger/Getty Images)

“Service members may request exemptions to any required vaccines through a service-level process,” a Department of War official told the DCNF. “We would refer to the respective military services departments for further, service-specific information.”

Marine Corps policy specifically barred the service from giving an enlisted Marine anything worse than a general discharge under honorable conditions when vaccine refusal was the sole basis for separation, according to official guidance issued in October 2021.

“When people ask me whether the military went too far, I point to what happened afterward,” Gary told the DCNF. “Years later, people like me are still trying to repair careers and records and obtain the relief that subsequent administrative and policy actions recognized was necessary. My case is an example of how correcting a piece of paper does not automatically restore the years of a person’s career that were lost.”

“For me, this isn’t an abstract debate about COVID policy anymore,” Gary said. “It is about what happens when the government damages a service member’s career and then makes that service member spend years fighting the same bureaucracy to actually receive the correction and relief they were granted.”

The Department of War later reached out to Marquis with an offer to amend his discharge documentation to an honorable discharge; however, that does not undo the time that Marquis spent in the “penal platoon” for nearly half a year.

Marquis said he objected to being classified as having “refused to train” and raised the issue with the Lima Company sergeant major, who offered to help expedite his administrative separation with an unfavorable discharge characterization. Marquis was not dishonorably discharged, however, and said he declined the offer so he could remain in the platoon and continue challenging the vaccine mandate.

“While the military has rescinded specific recent mandates like the COVID-19 vaccine, the overall policy governing standard service immunizations remains in effect,” a Marine Corps spokesperson told the DCNF. “Refusal of any mandatory military immunization without an officially approved medical, religious, or administrative waiver constitutes a violation of a lawful order and may result in disciplinary action including administrative separation or UCMJ action.”

Marquis was justified in his decision to refuse an unlawful order, and that similar violations of civil liberty still go on to this day, multiple legal experts told the DCNF. (RELATED: Netanyahu Dismissed Pre-Oct. 7 Hamas Warning, Never Told Top Security Officials)

“They have a right to object,” First Liberty Senior Counsel Chris Motz told the DCNF. “For objections based on religious grounds, the Religious Freedom Restoration Act gives strong protections, and requires the government to prove it has an interest in health and safety not just as a general concept, but as specifically applied to the individual objector, and that there are no other ways besides vaccination for it to satisfy that specific interest. This is a rigorous standard for the government to meet and often results in accommodations being granted, but not all the time. We are still seeing some vaccine accommodation requests being denied.”

“The Pentagon severely compromised operational readiness to enforce bureaucratic conformity,” Marcus Thornton, the Co-Founder of Feds For Freedom, told the DCNF. “Purging thousands of highly trained, specialized assets was a massive, self-inflicted vulnerability. Secretary Hegseth deserves credit for initiating necessary corrections to this disaster, but his efforts have not gone nearly far enough.”

More than 8,400 U.S. service members were discharged for refusing the COVID-19 vaccine before the Pentagon rescinded its military-wide mandate in January 2023, including 3,717 Marines, 2,041 sailors, 1,841 soldiers and 834 members of the Air Force and Space Force, according to Military Times, citing service data compiled in December 2022.

Only about 230, roughly 2.7% of those eligible, had rejoined by July 2026, Military Times reported, citing the Pentagon.

(Photo by United States Forces Korea via Getty Images)

“Service members may seek medical exemptions and religious accommodations,” a Michigan for Vaccine Choice spokesperson told the DCNF. “[Department of War] policy incorporates RFRA: a sincere religious belief must be accommodated unless the military shows a compelling interest and the least restrictive means. Medical contraindications are also recognized. A mandate does not erase those rights.”

“Service members do not surrender their constitutional rights when they put on the uniform,” Steve Crampton, senior counsel at the Thomas More Society, told the DCNF. “Both the First Amendment and the Religious Freedom Restoration Act require the military to give every sincere religious objection a fair, individualized hearing, and during the COVID-19 mandate, that didn’t happen.”

“I understand the military has legitimate responsibilities around readiness and protecting the force, but those responsibilities should not come at the expense of basic rights and meaningful due process,” Brianne Dressen, the co-chair of React 19, told the DCNF. “Service members who raised legitimate medical, religious, or conscience-based objections should have had their individual circumstances genuinely considered, rather than facing career-ending consequences simply for refusing one medical intervention.”

The military’s handling of religious exemptions also drew repeated legal challenges. In 2022, the Fifth Circuit Court of Appeals upheld an injunction protecting 35 Navy special warfare personnel who challenged the service’s handling of their religious accommodation requests, while other federal courts separately intervened in similar cases involving service members.

(Photo by JOSEPH PREZIOSO/AFP via Getty Images)

“Congress must enact explicit legal protections for both military and civilian federal workers that strictly prohibit blanket medical mandates which evade strict constitutional scrutiny,” Thornton told the DCNF. “We also need mandatory constitutional training for managers and commanders, coupled with severe, enforceable personal liability. When government leaders and managers violate the constitutional rights of their subordinates or the American people, they must face direct legal and financial consequences equal in impact to the consequences of their violations against others.”

While Trump’s command of the U.S. military did roll back changes made under the Biden administration, the significant lack of service members who were ousted by COVID requirements returning shows that it left a lasting impact on the armed forces.

“What this signals is that the state has allocated to itself a power that is entirely unheard of in American history until relatively recently,” Marquis told the DCNF. “This shows that the state, now that we’ve given it this power, is going to use it again.”

“People might say that COVID was five years ago, it doesn’t matter anymore, but that’s categorically wrong,” Marquis said. “This is more relevant than ever because now that the state has precedent for doing this. They’re going to do it again, and the next time it will be worse. They will keep pushing the envelope, keep expanding their power, and it is up to vigilant citizenry to try to interdict this in a peaceful but forceful manner before the liberties that we’ve cherished and passed on from generation to generation are lost to history.”

news.originalContent: The IDF addressed the strikes carried out overnight in southern Lebanon, including in the village of Kfar Reman, saying on Monday afternoon that they began after Hezbollah terrorists launched two explosive drones at Israeli forces on the Ali Taher ridge in southern Lebanon. No IDF troops were injured in the drone launches, and the military said it immediately began striking Hezbollah infrastructure in several areas across southern Lebanon, including what it said was a weapons storage facility.   No IDF troops were injured in the drone launches, and the military said it immediately began striking Hezbollah infrastructure in several areas across southern Lebanon, including what it said was a weapons storage facility. A vehicle in which two people were killed. The Associated Press reported that the vehicle belonged to the Lebanese Scout and Rescue Association, Al-Risala, and that one of those killed was a paramedic with the organization. Two other people were wounded. At the same time, Lebanese reports said a building in Kfar Reman where a large number of people were staying was also struck, killing nine people, including women and children, and wounding 11 others.   Prior to the strikes, steps were taken to mitigate harm to uninvolved individuals, including the use of precise munitions and aerial surveillance," the IDF said in response. "The claim that several uninvolved individuals were harmed as a result of the strikes is being reviewed.” The IDF said that, in addition, following the launch of the explosive drones Sunday, “the IDF struck in the Nabatieh area and eliminated several Hezbollah terrorists. "The IDF will not allow the Hezbollah terrorist organization to harm Israeli civilians or IDF soldiers and will continue to operate to remove threats while remaining committed to the ceasefire agreement." “We lived under constant intimidation because of the bombardments on the outskirts of the village,” Fouad Chakroun, a resident of Kfar Reman told AP as he stood in front of the destroyed building. “Now they have struck the heart of the village.” Another resident, Saleh Madlij, said families and children had been staying in the building. “Are there missiles here?” he said sarcastically. “I will not leave this place.” The BBC reported that, according to Lebanese media, seven additional people were killed in strikes Sunday, while Lebanese President Joseph Aoun warned that the attacks represented a “dangerous escalation” that threatened the ceasefire.

news.title: Israel's public diplomacy 'never been worse', officials say
news.originalSummary: Senior government officials admit that Israel's public opinion in the international community "has never been worse." According to them, the situation only worsens, and the support the world has shown Israel following Hamas’s attack on October 7 has already been forgotten. news.originalContent: Senior government officials admit that Israel's public opinion in the international community "has never been worse." According to them, the situation only worsens, and the support the world has shown Israel following Hamas’s attack on October 7 has already been forgotten.  Follow Ynetnews on Facebook | Twitter | Instagram | TikTok >> More stories: IDF releases name of fallen soldier in West Bank terror attack UN chief in Rafah crossing says world 'seen enough' of Gaza war Two Air Force pilots reminisce about their murdered brothers: 'There's no room for pain in the air' The officials added that the intensity of accusations made against Israel only increases, and attempts to equate Hamas's actions in Israel are being made, with allegations accusing IDF soldiers of sexually harassing Palestinian prisoners. Ministers in the government blame Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu for the complete neglect of Israel’s public relations: "There’s no leader present it’s been abandoned. A pandemic of sanctions against Israel may break out, and if we don't wake up, it will be too late. Something big needed to be done in terms of public relations, we need to rally the Jewish people and launch an international campaign. There’s no leader to head this. We’re losing. Our friends tell us: we support you, but you’re losing in the court of public opinion." A senior figure in Israel's advocacy efforts added, "They neutralized the Foreign Ministry and took away all its budget. The Foreign Ministry has no funding. To this day, no money was delivered. We’re working with a budget of 2 million shekels allocated for the war since the beginning of the year.  “Each U.S. consulate receives $5,000 a year for public relations efforts, including Independence Day events. For example, the consulate in Boston, which is also responsible for MIT, has to struggle to have such an amount. It’s ridiculous. When you already have a talented spokesman like Eylon Levy, they unjustly suspend him. He was one of the few people who did his mission in the most talented, beautiful, and correct way, and they sent him home,” the source said.   Internal reports from Israeli missions in the United States describe a very harsh picture of Israeli coverage in the American media. One report described, "The media awaited a sign from the government for a policy change, and when it arrived - it unleashed a rampage and published constant harsh criticism against Israel that had always existed. The harsh reports from Gaza, alongside internal tensions in the U.S., threaten to push moderate writers from the mainstream to adopt critical positions toward Israel and demand an immediate and permanent cease-fire.” 'the graphic images undermine the war’s legitimacy' “Pressure on the Biden administration to harden its stance toward Israel and condition military aid for an Israeli policy change constitutes a warning sign for the future,” the report added. “In terms of 'color,' we’re currently in a 'dark orange.' “There’s a change in stances even among staunch supporters of Israel – and while the conservative media fully supported Israel's actions in the past, this time voices questioning the proportionality of Israeli action have also been heard. However, no demand for a cease-fire is expected to appear in those media outlets. Without a fundamental change in the humanitarian issue in Gaza and/or signs on the diplomatic solution on the horizon, criticism of Israel in the media is expected to intensify,” the report read. It was added, "In the last month, the U.S. media’s spotlight turned to the worsening humanitarian crisis in Gaza, with special emphasis given to the suffering of Rafah residents against the backdrop of the possibility of the IDF expanding the ground operation there as well. Leading media outlets flooded screens and front pages with images of starving children, trauma victims, and the destruction of homes and hospitals. Reports and personal stories from Rafah led to empathy toward the Palestinians’ suffering and anger toward Israel's military actions. "Although most media outlets refrained from blaming Israel for creating the crisis intentionally or denying its right to self-defense, opinion pieces sparked fierce debate regarding the proportionality and morality of the ongoing military operation in its current form. Critical voices that were once silenced now have a wider platform.    “Reports focused on the immense humanitarian damages and the harm to innocent civilians, which many analysts argue is unjustified and goes against the values of the IDF’s operation. Even publicists who supported Israel in the past admitted that the graphic images undermine the war’s legitimacy,” the report read. “Against this backdrop, a narrative is emerging among liberal authors, which sees the Biden administration and its policy of providing weapons and diplomatic support to Israel as responsible for the situation, or at least as someone who can bring it to an end." Furthermore, dozens of recent opinion pieces represent a wide range of positions regarding the IDF’s legitimacy, the humanitarian crisis in Gaza, the question of a cease-fire, and the future of U.S.-Israel relations: Conservative media outlets like The Wall Street Journal and The New York Post fully support Israel, advocate for continued military action against Hamas, and refrain from calling for an immediate and prolonged stop to the war.  In contrast, newspapers identified with the center and liberal left, including The New York Times and The Washington Post, criticize the war’s escalation, citing the destructive consequences of the confrontation on Palestinian civilians, and therefore calling for an immediate humanitarian cease-fire, the reports explained.   The reports also expose an erosion of Israel's standing in Washington against the backdrop of the escalation in the Gaza war. This was clearly reflected in U.S. President Joe Biden's statement regarding a "red line" on military operations in Rafah, and Senate Majority Leader Chuck Schumer's speech.  Most analysts don’t foresee an immediate shift in relations between the countries, but caution against potential political damage to both sides. Furthermore, calls are increasing to use American military aid to Israel as leverage to force policy change in Jerusalem. However, warnings have been raised that the fact of having this discussion could bolster Hamas's position and undermine the chances of a cease-fire.  While conservative media outlets present Israel's policy as legitimate self-defense, liberal media outlets provide a platform for writers who echo the Palestinian narrative, sometimes using rhetoric accusing Israel of "apartheid" and even "genocide." Calls for the U.S. government to distance itself from supporting Israel and reconsider its military aid plan are becoming more common, even in moderate media outlets. The report mentions articles in The Washington Post and The Daily Beast highlighting the effectiveness of pro-Palestinian activists in influencing public opinion in the U.S., especially among progressive Democratic voters. The articles point to growing discontent with the Biden administration's support for Israel, reflected in "Uncommitted" votes in the Democratic primaries and disruptions at party events. Tactics such as demanding a cease-fire and using the term "genocide" have succeeded in keeping the war at the forefront of the national political agenda and increasing pressure on Washington to minimize its support of Israel.  The increasing willingness of Democratic politicians to criticize Israel suggests a shift in the party's traditional stance and leads to speech free of restraint in media outlets as well. This trend reached its zenith with Senate Majority Leader Chuck Schumer's speech, in which he labeled Netanyahu an "obstacle to peace" and accused him of damaging Israel's international standing, calling for early Israeli elections.

news.originalTitle: 'We are in Shock': British Jews react to fatal terror attack - and fume at the 'lax response' of the UK
news.title: 'We are in Shock': British Jews react to fatal terror attack - and fume at the 'lax response' of the UK
news.originalSummary: Rather than celebrating and resting over the three-day holiday, residents of the Jewish community of Hendon in north London and Radlett were struck by shock and grief after the deadly terror attack that took the lives of two daughters of their beloved and esteemed Rabbi Leo Dee, on Friday, the second day of Passover which is considered a holly day in diaspora communities. news.originalContent: Rather than celebrating and resting over the three-day holiday, residents of the Jewish community of Hendon in north London and Radlett were struck by shock and grief after the deadly terror attack that took the lives of two daughters of their beloved and esteemed Rabbi Leo Dee, on Friday, the second day of Passover which is considered a holly day in diaspora communities.   Follow Ynetnews on Facebook and Twitter >> Related stories: Israel names two sisters killed in West Bank terror attack At least one dead and six injured in a terror attack in Tel Aviv Family loses two daughters to deadly terror attack Members of the Jewish London community, including friends of the family, who heard of the devastating news after the Shabbat ended, were confronted only then, with the horrific reports of Maia and Rina's death. The funerals for the Dee sisters will be held today at the Kfar Etzion Cemetery.   Rabbi Leo Dee served as the Assistant Rabbi at the Hendon United Synagogue in North London from 2008-2011, and as the Senior Rabbi at Radlett United Synagogue from 2011-2014, after which the family made aliyah. They were a much beloved and respected family in the UK Jewish community. “People feel shock and disappointment. The family were communal people and served their communities well and were well-liked.” said a former member of the congregation at Hendon United Synagogue who did not wish to be named.  “I feel sick seeing this… good people who would never hurt anyone, murdered. I can't imagine his anguish, and pray Lucy survives,” said Joseph, another former congregant.   Chief UK Rabbi Sir Ephraim Mirvis laments the death of the British-Israeli girls murdered in Friday's terror strike on the West Bank.  In a statement, the rabbi said: "No words can describe the depth of our shock and sadness at the heartbreaking news of the murder by terrorists in Israel of Maya & Rina Dee, daughters of Rebbetzen Lucy, who is in a critical condition & Rabbi Leo Dee, my dear colleagues. He continued, “They were much loved in the Hendon and Radlett communities in the UK, as well as in Israel and well beyond.” UK statement not mentioning terrorism The British Board of Deputies also issued a statement expressing shock over the tragic attack: “We are deeply shocked and saddened at the murder by Palestinian terrorists of Maia and Rina Dee, the daughters of Rabbi Leo and Lucy Dee formerly of Radlett United Synagogue. We wish Lucy Refuah Shlemah and long life to the family as they cope with this devastating news.” Palestinian terrorist shot and killed 2 British-Israeli nationals, also critically injuring their mother in the West Bank. The victims were identified Saturday as 15-year-old Rina Dee and 20-year-old Maia Dee, the daughters of British-born Rabbi Leo Dee.  While their mother, Lucy (Lea), remains in critical condition fighting for her life, the Jewish community in the UK has expressed shock and sorrow at the brutal act of terrorism against former members of their community.    While many Jewish community leaders spoke out about the attack, the UK government has received criticism from some members of the community for its weakly-worded response to the killing of two of its own citizens.  One member of the Jewish community told Ynet that it was shocking that the UK statement didn’t even mention terrorism. “The response would be different if this happened elsewhere in the world. There is a double standard for British people killed in Israel,” he said.  The UK’s official statement read: “We are saddened to hear about the deaths of two British-Israeli citizens and the serious injuries sustained by a third individual. The UK calls for all parties across the region to de-escalate tensions.” "Tragedy for global Jewish community" Avi Abelow, family friend, said Rabbi Leo and Lucy Dee are beloved and active members of their community in Efrat. "Two of the sweetest people with the sweetest children", he added. "Rabbi Leo continues to teach Torah classes in his Efrat synagogue today. All the youth of Efrat, as their families, are mourning the loss of either their personal friend or the sibling of their personal friend."  He mentioned that "Just last night the whole community got together, including many youth, for a special communal prayer gathering to pray for Lucy's recovery. The brutal Arab Muslim terrorist attack that murdered these two young, innocent Jewish women, and seriously injured their mother fighting for her life, is not just a tragedy for their family, but for the whole Efrat community and the global Jewish community.  "At the same time that another terrorist committed a terror attack in Tel Aviv, which killed an Italian tourist, and terrorist organizations are shooting rockets at Israel from Lebanon, Syria and Gaza, we are once again reminded that the Jewish people have enemies trying to kill us everywhere in our country for just being Jews living in our ancestral homeland.  "If only the UK government and other global bodies would recognize this truth, and truly give support to Israel to stop this ongoing terror war against Israel, which causes loss of life for everyone. In the meantime, as a personal friend and neighbor of the Dee family, my family, neighbors, and community will continue to assist and comfort the Dee family, as we assisted and comforted the family of our other friend and neighbor, Ari Fuld, murdered by terrorists back in 2018."

news.originalContent:

Ukrainian tennis pro Elina Svitolina explained that her decision to end her and Gaël Monfil’s marriage came down to more than Russia’s war in her native country.

The pair announced they were ending their marriage of five years in a joint Instagram post Monday, in which Svitolina, 32, shared she lost herself in the ongoing war and “with time, I came to understand that I need to find my way back to myself and that I cannot do that within our marriage.”

In another statement Tuesday, Svitolina further “clarified” her decision — and she explained that the 40-year-old Frenchman retired earlier than expected due to their divorce.

“I just want to clarify my previous post a little, because I realized that not everyone, especially my international audience, fully understood what I was trying to say,” Svitolina, who is ranked world No. 6, wrote.

“In that post, I shared only one of the reasons that influenced my decision and made me reflect on my life and my future. But the truth is, there’s so much more to it, and it was never just about one thing.

“When you’ve been living through the reality of war for more than 4.5 years, experiencing so many different situations, emotions, and difficult moments, you naturally start seeing life differently. Your perspective changes, your values and priorities shift, and you begin to understand what you truly want out of life.”

Svitolina and Monfils, who got married in Switzerland in July 2021, share a daughter named, Skaï, born in October 2022.

“At some point, I simply realized that I didn’t want to keep living a life where I wasn’t truly happy,” she said. “And believe me, coming to this decision was anything but easy. I love and respect my husband very much. And I will always love and appreciate him for the person he is. That’s exactly why it was so important for me to be honest, both with him and with myself.

“It’s not always possible to explain everything behind such personal and difficult decisions in a single post. And honestly, some things are simply too personal to share publicly. That was and is my view on announcing the end of our marriage but as some of you saw, Gael’s career ended abruptly after he made the decision to stop based on our situation. Unfortunately he had many accusations thrown at him and he didn’t deserve that, so we jointly released a statement.

“I just hope this helps you understand a little better what I was trying to say but please be kind and understanding, this is incredibly tough for us both right now 💔”.

Monfils — who previously announced last year that he would retire after a 22-year career at the Paris Masters in November — was registered as retired by the International Tennis Integrity Agency (ITIA) on Oct. 5.

The 13-time ATP Tour singles champion withdrew from a wild card spot at the ATP 250 event in Lyon on Monday for “personal reasons,” the tournament said.

Monfils played his last professional match Sept. 3, losing in the second round of the US Open to Learner Tien (6–3, 6–4, 6–3).

The two reached the US Open mixed doubles semi-finals together in August.

Svitolina is the midst of a stellar 2026 campaign.

Sam Altman on Tuesday won the dismissal of a civil lawsuit filed by his sister accusing the OpenAI co-founder and chief executive of repeated sexual abuse more than two decades ago, an accusation he denies.

In dismissing Annie Altman’s lawsuit, US District Judge Zachary Bluestone wrote that she had refused to appear for an independent medical examination despite warnings that failure to do so would result in the case’s dismissal.

Laura Politi, a lawyer for Annie Altman, did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Santos Perez, a lawyer who previously represented Annie Altman in the case but withdrew this month, said in a statement, “I am no longer authorized to comment on this case but I continue to believe in Annie.”

Lawyers for Sam Altman did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Sam Altman became a face of the artificial intelligence boom after the chatbot ChatGPT was released in 2022.

Annie Altman brought her lawsuit in St. Louis federal court in January 2025.

She accused her brother of sexually abusing and raping her between 1997 and 2006 at the family home in suburban Clayton, Mo., starting when she was 3 and he was 12.

She said the last acts of sexual abuse and rape occurred when Sam Altman was an adult. He is now 41.

The Altman family has said Annie Altman has mental health challenges and received financial support.

Sam Altman has said she began accusing him on social media of sexual abuse after the family rejected her demands for more funds.

news.originalContent:
See more of our coverage in your search results.

An unexpected shot of bad news.

A popular weight-loss shot has been recalled across the country by the FDA due to potential contamination.

The US-based compounding pharmacy that issued the initial recall back in September had already been on the agency’s radar and previously received a warning.

Apothecary Pharma, a compounding pharmacy based in North Carolina, is recalling 22 vials of their compounded tirzepatide, the active ingredient in Mounjaro and Zepbound, though these brand name drugs aren’t affected by the recall.

Even if you didn’t buy directly from Apothecary Pharma, your medication could still be affected.

The company reportedly supplies compounded tirzepatide to several telehealth providers, so check your vial’s label for the manufacturer and lot number.

Recalled vials are labeled 18 mg/mL in a 4 mL multi-dose vial.

Apothecary Pharma is also recalling a NAD+ injection, a popular longevity supplement, for possible contamination.

Both recalls are Class II, which means that using these products could cause “temporary or medically reversible adverse health consequences” though severe health consequences are unlikely.

This is not the first time the FDA has disciplined Apothecary Pharma for this reason.

In December, they issued a warning letter to the company after an inspection found “serious deficiencies in your practices for producing drug products intended or expected to be sterile, which put patients at risk.”

The FDA regulates sterility at every stage of production — from cleanroom airflow and equipment cleaning to personnel gowning and filtration — not just through final-product testing.

“Lack of assurance of sterility” means the FDA cannot guarantee the product is free of contamination because of compromised sterility at some point in the production chain.

In this case, the federal agency saw operators improperly handling sterile containers, touching sterile work areas and failing to change gloves to prevent contamination, and noted visibly rusty and hard-to-clean equipment.

Compounding services like Apothecary Pharma offer alternative formulations of brand-name drugs, originally for medication shortages and specialized patient needs. However, it’s become a way for manufacturers to get around strict FDA regulations and offer steep discounts.

While most people on GLP-1s use the brand name stuff, as many as 5 million are on compounded versions. Many people get these compounded versions through telehealth companies, which ship them directly to patients.

Compounded drugs are not reviewed for safety, effectiveness or quality before they’re put on the market.

The FDA has flagged dosing errors from compounded GLP-1s that landed people in the hospital, improper storage that doesn’t keep them cool enough and even fraudulent compounded drugs listing a manufacturer that doesn’t exist.

The agency also expressed concerns about multi-dose vials, which were included in this recall, as they rely on patients to self-administer doses from a vial that could become contaminated, especially after 28 days.

The FDA has received more than 730 reports of bad reactions to compounded tirzepatide, the drug implicated in this recall — though they say this is likely underreported.

The annual UCL clash of the year is set as back-to-back Champions League winners Paris Saint-Germain host Barcelona in a league-stage showdown Tuesday.

As expected, these two teams sit atop the UEFA standings at 2-0, with PSG’s 10 goals leading the way and Barca’s nine tied for second-best with Ashton Villa.

Both teams are masters of scoring, with PSG averaging three goals per game in their last six wins and Barca scoring 48 goals in 11 games.

PSG enters Matchday 3 in rejuvenated form and ready to defend home turf at the Parc des Princes.

The French club stumbled out of the gate and is 2-2-1 in Ligue 1, but has turned things up a notch in the league phase.

Luis Enrique’s squad opened their UCL campaign with a 6-1 win over Slovan Bratislava, then impressively beat Erling Haaland and Man City 4-2 at the Etihad Stadium last week.

Reigning Ballon d’Or winner Ousmane Dembélé, Spain’s World Cup hero Ferran Torres, Khvicha Kvaratskhelia, Achraf Hakimi and young star Désiré Doué lead the way.

On the other side of the field, Barça’s well-oiled machine recently beat Real Betis 5-2 to reach 11 straight wins.

Blaugrana also rallied after falling behind early to beat Galatasaray 4-1 in Turkey last Tuesday, and they made quick work of Feyenoord on UCL Matchday 1.

PSG will do everything it can to keep Hansi Flick’s squad from dominating possession because there is really no other way to keep Barca’s elaborate attack at bay.

An underlying rivalry also stems from offseason trash talk between Dembélé and Lamine Yamal over who should’ve been named Ballon d’Or last year.

Dembélé has backed his name, netting three goals and providing three assists in two UCL games. Yamal enters with one goal and four assists across two UCL fixtures.

Factor in that PSG manager Enrique played 207 games for Barca over more than eight years, rejoined as coach for another three years and led the Spain national team at the 2022 World Cup before stepping down, and this becomes appointment viewing.

news.originalContent:
See more of our coverage in your search results.

Bryan Kohberger’s new lawyer is taking another swing at Idaho prosecutors in his fight to have the judge who called his client a “faceless coward” removed from post-conviction proceedings.

Court-appointed attorney Greg Rauch is accusing Latah County prosecutors of “regurgitating” rules rather than addressing concerns raised in his motion to disqualify Judge Steven Hippler from the case.

Hippler said Kohberger, 31, “slithered” into the victims’ home before committing a crime that made him “the worst of the worst” after the killer admitted guilt last year.

At issue, according to Rauch, “is how [Hippler’s] statements about counsel’s preparation and [Kohberger’s] capacity for truthfulness bear on the disputes it may now decide, in combination with the myriad of other statements made.”

And when addressing the fact that there would be no allocution or explanation from Kohberger, the judge also questioned whether Kohberger even possessed the capacity to say something truthful.

“Even if I could force him to speak, which legally I cannot, how could anyone ever be assured that what he speaks is the truth?” Hippler asked during sentencing. “Do we really believe, after all of this, he is capable of speaking the truth, or of giving up something of himself to help the very people whose lives he destroyed? Rather, I suspect the so-called reason would be dished out in enticing self-serving and aggrandizing untruthful bits, leaving people wanting more information, more insight, and thus enhancing even further the power he seeks to hold.”

Rauch wrote that “of course” judges can deny defense motions, “condemn terrible crimes,” and go on to preside over post-conviction claims.

“The question is not whether someone might criticize the Court, but whether an informed, reasonable observer could question its impartiality in light of this connected record,” he wrote.

And it’s not just that Hippler tore into Kohberger at sentencing. He has also taken issue with a June scheduling order days before Kohberger surprised the country and pleaded guilty to avoid the death penalty.

“This motion does not rest upon one adverse ruling, one harsh statement, or the mere fact that the judge who presided over Bryan Kohberger’s criminal case has been assigned to his post-conviction proceeding,” Rauch wrote in his initial 22-page motion on Aug. 27. “It rests upon the extraordinary convergence of all of them.”

Hippler had rejected a request for more time for Kohberger’s previous defense lawyer, Anne Taylor, and in a June 26 order, described her complaints about discovery as “ultimately empty” while suggesting she was simply trying to delay his trial.

Six days later, at a change-of-plea hearing, Hippler asked Taylor, “Have you been able to do all the discovery you feel necessary?”

“Yes, Your Honor,” she replied.

Prosecutors, in an opposition to the motion filed earlier this month, wrote that Kohberger had failed to show Hippler “is biased.”

Outgoing Latah County Prosecuting Attorney Bill Thompson, who announced his retirement earlier this week, and Deputy Prosecuting Attorney Keith Scholl wrote that Hippler’s statements about Kohberger after he’d admitted to killing four innocent students were not unusual or out of line.

“In our case, the sentencing remarks are not enough to show bias, and the required showing of perceived bias cannot be tied to this Court’s capacity to fairly adjudicate any [post-conviction relief] claims alleged in this case but rather puts this Court in the best position to adjudicate them as the legislature and the Idaho Supreme Court’s rules intend,” they wrote.

Rauch also argued that Hippler could voluntarily recuse himself from the case to avoid any appearance of partiality.

In the new 12-page filing, Rauch also argued that prosecutors have attributed concessions to his client that were never made, mischaracterized his initial motion and failed to address some of the arguments he did make in it.

“The State’s Response does not resolve this motion by repeating the ordinary rule, supplying concessions Petitioner never made, or calling the disputed statements routine,” Rauch wrote.

Kohberger is attempting to undo his guilty plea in the University of Idaho student murders that killed Madison Mogen, 21, Kaylee Goncalves, 21, Xana Kernodle, 20, and Ethan Chapin, 20, in November 2022.

The former criminology Ph.D. student initially filed a handwritten petition for post-conviction relief in July.

“The State’s Response does not resolve this motion by repeating the ordinary rule, supplying concessions Petitioner never made, or calling the disputed statements routine,” Rauch wrote.

“A request for an impartial adjudicator is certainly not a request for a sympathetic one,” he wrote. “Reassignment would change the judge, not the evidence or the governing law.”

A hearing on the matter was supposed to take place Thursday, before Hippler abruptly canceled it and said it would be rescheduled later.

news.originalContent:
Calls for independence intensified last year, with some 300,000 petitioning officials for a referendum.

Voters in Alberta have chosen to remain part of Canada in a first-ever independence referendum.

Canadian state broadcaster CBC News called the results of Monday’s vote late on the same day after 48 percent of the ballots counted showed overwhelming support for the “remain” side, with 76 percent opting to stay with Canada.

The result marks a major win for Prime Minister Mark Carney, who is facing a trade and political war with the United States amid US President Donald Trump’s higher tariffs and repeated suggestions of annexing the country.

On his way into a cabinet meeting on Tuesday morning, Carney called it a “great day.”

“I’m thrilled that Albertans have chosen unity. They’ve chosen to build together. They’ve chosen to continue to take care of each other, to move forward together with purpose,” he said.

But the result also comes as a disappointment for those Albertans seeking independence for the resource-rich region following years of grievances laid at Ottawa’s door. Here’s what we know:

The nonbinding referendum was first announced in May following a campaign and petition by a group of Albertans who want to be an independent country.

While only about one-third of Albertans were found to be pro-independence in polls, Alberta Premier Danielle Smith argued in her announcement that a referendum was necessary to respect the 300,000 Albertans who had petitioned officials for it.

In the referendum, voters answered 10 questions, including whether the government should begin a binding process to seek independence from Canada. They also answered questions on immigration, access to provincial services like education, social care and healthcare, and voter identification requirements.

Prime Minister Carney had campaigned for Albertans to vote “remain”, saying last week at a rally in Calgary that separation would be “ a dangerous bluff that will lead to years of deep division”.

“There are some outside our borders who are working to break us so they can own us,” he said.

Researchers have pointed to possible online influence campaigns by both Russian and US entities that helped amplify the call for separation and allegedly shared misleading information. Alberta PM Smith told media in August that the online activity was under observation.

Prime Minister Carney, who grew up in the region, said “Albertans made a clear choice” in a statement he made early on Tuesday.

“They chose unity, to build together, and to take care of each other,” he said, adding that “Canadians will move forward together with renewed purpose and high ambition.”

Alberta’s Premier Smith said she was pleased to see the results and that “Albertans have voted for a stronger Alberta in a united Canada.”

Separatist leaders from the groups Let Alberta Decide, the Alberta Prosperity Project and the Pathway to Independence said they will wait for all votes to be counted before conceding.

First Nations groups turned out in strong numbers to vote to remain with Canada, with one southern Alberta polling station in an area home to the Siksika Nation temporarily running out of ballots, local media reported.

Many Albertans have long complained that their critical natural resources are funding the government in Ottawa and the commercial hubs of Toronto and Montreal, but that the province does not receive proportionate benefits.

The province, with a population of 5.1 million, holds massive oil deposits. It also holds reserves of critical and rare-earth metals including lithium, titanium and zircon, which are essential for manufacturing many tech items, from smartphones to fighter jets.

Separatist movements, some of which even support Alberta joining the US, go back to the 1940s, following the discovery of oil reserves. Some of Alberta’s premiers have had spats with Ottawa over wealth distribution.

US President Trump has made remarks about Canada becoming a US state in recent months.

Last week, he told a political rally in the US state of Arizona that Canada will “end up being the 51st state, because it’s the only way it works”.

The two countries have been embroiled in a trade war since talks fell apart in August this year and they slapped each other with tit-for-tat tariffs.

Earlier this month, tech billionaire Elon Musk called for Alberta, Saskatchewan and Quebec to separate from Canada, saying “they’d be better off”.

But the matter of Alberta’s independence gained intense scrutiny last year after pro-separatists launched a petition to pressure the government.

Alberta, alongside other western provinces of British Columbia, Saskatchewan and Manitoba, have all complained about “western alienation” by the government in the centre.

With separatism agitations running so far back, experts say the referendum will likely not end the movement altogether.

Ahead of the vote, some separatist leaders said they would pursue another referendum if necessary, arguing that the referendum shows that independence is legally possible.

“Regardless of what happens on Monday, we’ve already won,” Keith Wilson, co-leader of Let Alberta Decide, said at a rally last week.

news.originalContent:
With new talk of escalation, Islamabad is trying to revive negotiations without alienating Tehran, Riyadh or Washington.

Islamabad, Pakistan – Pakistan’s army chief, Field Marshal Asim Munir, arrived in Tehran on Tuesday evening for talks with Iranian officials, as diplomatic efforts ramp up to prevent a new round of fighting with the United States and Israel.

Munir’s visit is his fifth to Iran since the April ceasefire between Tehran and Washington, which was brokered by Islamabad. Pakistan’s Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi is accompanying Munir, Iran’s state news agency IRNA reported. The Pakistani army chief is expected to meet Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi first, IRNA said.

The visit comes a day after Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov held talks in Tehran, and two weeks after Pakistan and its allies agreed to accelerate the deployment of forces to Saudi Arabia, which has come under repeated attacks from the Iran-backed Houthi armed group in Yemen.

Lavrov’s visit on Monday was his first to Tehran since the start of the US-Israel war on Iran in February. The Russian foreign minister met Araghchi and President Masoud Pezeshkian, and the talks covered the war, the Strait of Hormuz and efforts to end the fighting.

“The timing of [Munir’s] visit, following Lavrov’s presence in Tehran, suggests that Iran prefers to keep multiple diplomatic channels open, rather than relying exclusively on a single mediator,” Seyed Mojtaba Jalazadeh, a Tehran-based foreign policy analyst, told Al Jazeera.

But the Munir visit also comes at a time when some experts have warned of growing signs that United States President Donald Trump might be preparing for a return to fighting with Iran. Trump rejected an Iranian proposal to end the war on September 26. Since then, the US has deployed an additional aircraft carrier to the Middle East, which is expected to arrive by late November. Trump has endorsed Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu in Israel’s upcoming October 27 election, referring to their shared mission in attacking Iran. Trump said that if Netanyahu were not re-elected, the US would need to attack Iran on its own.

Analysts say these developments add urgency to diplomatic efforts to sidestep a potential military escalation. In recent weeks, Qatar has played a key role in channeling proposals between the US and Iran. Andreas Krieg, an associate professor in security studies at King’s College London, told Al Jazeera that while Qatar increasingly provides the diplomatic machinery behind the talks, Doha still values Islamabad’s access to Washington and Tehran.

“Pakistan offers political access, particularly through Field Marshal Asim Munir, while Qatar does much of the detailed negotiating,” Krieg said.

Pakistan has mediated between Washington and Tehran since the US and Israel began striking Iran on February 28.

Islamabad brokered a ceasefire on April 8 and, days later, hosted the highest-level direct engagement between the US and Iran since 1979.

In June, the two sides agreed to a 14-point memorandum of understanding (MoU).

Under the agreement, the US was to lift its naval blockade within 30 days, the Strait of Hormuz was to reopen, and about $24bn in estimated frozen Iranian assets was to be released in phases over 60 days of further talks, including negotiations on Iran’s nuclear programme.

That period expired in mid-August without either side agreeing to extend it. Iran says the US failed to meet its commitments, and Tehran has kept the Strait of Hormuz closed, insisting that Washington first lift the blockade.

Pakistan’s Foreign Office has continued to point to the agreement and its utility.

“The Islamabad MoU is already in place, and some of the points currently under discussion are fully aligned with it,” spokesman Sajjad Haider Khan told a weekly briefing on October 9.

Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar said on October 2 that Iran’s seven-day plan was drawn from the MoU.

Analysts, however, disagree on whether the agreement can still provide a basis for negotiations.

“On the Islamabad MoU, I think it’s done from both sides and perhaps a new mechanism is required to start negotiations,” Umer Karim, an associate fellow at the King Faisal Centre for Research and Islamic Studies in Riyadh, told Al Jazeera.

Krieg said that while the Islamabad MoU was “politically alive”, it was “operationally dead”.

“The circumstances under which it was signed have fundamentally changed,” he said.

But Muhammad Faisal, a South Asia security researcher at the University of Technology Sydney, said the agreement could still be used.

“The Islamabad MoU remains usable, even if the political and security environment has deteriorated,” he told Al Jazeera. “It is still the minimum agreed benchmark between Washington and Tehran, and neither side has an obvious alternative framework for addressing the issues related to maritime access, sanctions relief and nuclear talks.”

Meanwhile, Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and Turkiye signed the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement on August 7.

It was Pakistan’s second defence pact with Saudi Arabia, after the Strategic Mutual Defence Agreement the two countries signed in September 2025.

At an emergency meeting in Riyadh on October 5, the three countries agreed to expedite the deployment of forces and capabilities under the pact.

Within days, Houthi missiles and drones struck Riyadh’s King Khalid international airport more than once, as well as targets in Abha, Yanbu and Shaybah.

Lieutenant-General Ahmed Sharif Chaudhry, the Pakistani military’s spokesman, discussed the defence pact and the importance of protecting holy sites in Mecca and Medina in an interview with Independent Arabia on October 18.

“The security of the Harmain Sharifain is paramount. It’s non-negotiable,” he said, referring to Islam’s two holiest mosques. “Whatever support is needed to do that is being provided and will be provided.”

He declined to provide details, citing operational confidentiality.

Munir’s visit is his fifth to Iran since the April ceasefire between Tehran and Washington, which was brokered by Islamabad. Pakistan’s Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi is accompanying Munir, Iran’s state news agency IRNA reported. The Pakistani army chief is expected to meet Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi first, IRNA said.

The visit comes a day after Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov held talks in Tehran, and two weeks after Pakistan and its allies agreed to accelerate the deployment of forces to Saudi Arabia, which has come under repeated attacks from the Iran-backed Houthi armed group in Yemen.

news.originalContent:
The UK’s new prime minister has made big promises and is a popular leader, but there is still talk of an early election.

Andy Burnham’s UK foreign policy tested by Brexit, US ties and Iran war

London, United Kingdom – There was a moment towards the end of Andy Burnham’s conference speech in Liverpool that, through silence, spoke volumes.

The new prime minister and Labour leader fell quiet.

For 20 seconds he stood, saying nothing. He hadn’t forgotten his words. He was gathering his emotions for a passage of the speech he hadn’t been able to make it through in rehearsals without crying.

Burnham’s father had died just a couple of weeks before, and this was the section where he’d talk about it.

As the audience realised what was coming they stood, applauding, and urging him on with shouts of “Come on, lad!’ and “Come on, Andy!”

Thanking them, he composed himself and continued.

Conference speeches are theatre, and contemporary British political standards require that a leader be relatable. But there’s little doubt that Andy Burnham handled this moment with an emotional register that struck many as genuine.

His predecessor Keir Starmer sometimes came across as wooden, almost robotic and uncomfortable in front of cameras. Burnham, the seventh prime minister in 10 years, is more emotional.

He talks big ideas and grand solutions and relishes the opportunity to communicate.

In the vibes-denominated currency of modern political discourse, this matters.

The polls speak for themselves. Politico’s Poll of Polls had the Labour Party retake top spot shortly after Burnham became PM – a position it has not relinquished since. At the end of September, Ipsos found Andy Burnham to be the only politician with a positive net favourability rating.

YouGov’s polling also judges him the most popular politician in the UK at the moment.

But to keep up, Burnham must deliver tangible change before the next general election. Unless he calls one early, that will be 2029.

According to political analyst Sam Freedman, “So many in Westminster keep coming back to an early election, despite Burnham ruling it out … No one can quite figure out how Burnham keeps the hope vibe going for three more years with relatively little visible progress.”

In the Welsh town of Port Talbot, terraces of workers’ cottages cluster beside the UK’s largest steelworks.

Like much of Wales, Port Talbot did vote Labour for a century – until elections for the Senedd Cymru or Welsh Parliament in May.

Labour was beaten to an unprecedented third place behind Plaid Cymru’s nationalists, and the anti-immigration Reform UK.

But that was before Burnham took over.

Myles Lewis, who organises social walks for the town’s elderly, told Al Jazeera that Labour had not convinced people on immigration, and Starmer’s communication wasn’t good enough.

“[But now], it’s kind of going back to what Labour was in the 50s and 60s, where they actually looked after the working-class people. I do believe Andy Burnham can get there because I think he has the interests of the working-class people.”

In his first weeks in power, Burnham delivered a quick flurry of eye-catching, domestic, cost-of-living-focused policies.

He capped bus fares, cut the value-added tax (VAT) on electricity bills, and cut business rates for pubs.

He said that he would end street homelessness, reindustrialise the country, take services back into public control, and start the biggest build-out of social housing since World War II.

The mayor of Greater Manchester for nine years, Burnham supports the devolution of powers from Westminster to the UK’s nations and regions.

In July, he announced mayors could keep a share of business rates from April 2027 and of income tax from 2028.

And his conference speech in September set out the contours of some big political battles to come, including a national social care service, free at the point of use, paid for by changing the UK pensions’ triple lock from 2030. It would arrive next parliament. Burnham also pitched a national commission on electoral reform, with a manifesto commitment to overhaul the voting system. And he delivered a blunt verdict on Brexit: that it “has done more harm than good”. He wouldn’t rule out an in-out referendum, or a pledge for the UK to rejoin the European Union, in Labour’s next manifesto, he said.

On foreign affairs, there is less blue water between Burnham and his predecessors.

When he travelled to Ukraine in August, the UK’s new prime minister came with a headline-grabbing gift – British know-how to build the long-range SCALP missile. He was the fourth British prime minister to visit Kyiv since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine and pledge steadfast support.

On Gaza, he has said the Labour government “didn’t get it right” and should have called for a ceasefire earlier. And in September, the Burnham government announced a sanctions package against illegal West Bank settlements.

But there has been no genocide declaration, and no full arms embargo against Israel. And Burnham hasn’t overturned the Starmer government’s proscription of the Palestine Action protest group as a “terrorist” organisation.

Defence spending is also a looming problem.

The government’s formal defence pledge is 3.5 percent of gross domestic product (GDP) by 2035, and Burnham has declined to say whether he’d pay for it with tax rises or welfare cuts.

John Healey, who resigned as the UK’s defence secretary in June over underfunding, is now chancellor of the exchequer, and will not commit to the 3-percent-by-2030 target he set himself.

Burnham’s first budget comes at the end of this month. A full spending review follows next year. Much will be clearer after these.

His biggest pledges – reindustrialisation, control of public services, a new social care system – are expensive.

Burnham certainly has the vibes. The public likes them, for now. The budget will show whether he can afford them.

news.originalContent:
UNICEF says escalating fighting in Taiz is threatening its water systems, serving an estimated three million people.

More than 250,000 people have been internally displaced in Yemen since the country’s war reignited in July, the United Nations Refugee Agency (UNHCR) has said, as fighting between Houthi rebels and forces loyal to the internationally recognised government rages across several fronts.

The city of Taiz in southwestern Yemen is at the centre of the displacement crisis, accounting for 76 percent of departures and hosting 52 percent of those newly displaced, UNHCR said in a statement on Tuesday.

Lahij in southwestern Yemen hosts 23 percent of the newly displaced population, followed by Aden in the south with 13 percent, UNHCR said.

“Shelling intensified in Taiz, including in residential areas and around health facilities, while insecurity and restrictions along key routes continue to constrain humanitarian access and movement,” the agency said in a statement.

The Houthis, an armed group also known as Ansar Allah (Arabic for Supporters of God), have encircled Taiz since early October, blocking the road that links it to Aden, the interim capital of the Saudi-backed internationally recognised government.

“The most immediate needs that we’ve been able to identify are around shelter, food, and multi-purpose cash assistance,” UNHCR spokesperson Matthew Saltmarsh told a news conference in Geneva, Switzerland.

The agency said about 33,700 families still require shelter assistance amid severe underfunding of the humanitarian response to the war.

Separately, the UN Children’s Fund (UNICEF) said in a statement that escalating fighting and fuel shortages in Taiz are threatening its water systems that serve an estimated three million people, including at least 1.6 million children.

“Already one of Yemen’s most water-scarce areas, Taiz is now facing renewed pressure on its most essential services for thousands of displaced families,” said Akhil Iyer, UNICEF’s Yemen representative, at a press briefing in Geneva.

The warnings come as fighting intensifies between Saudi-backed government forces and the Iran-aligned Houthis.

The death toll from a Houthi ballistic missile strike on a military training camp in Yemen’s Shabwa governorate increased to at least 58, local authorities said.

The Yemeni government described the site as a security training centre away from the front lines, while Houthi forces said they targeted Saudi-backed forces. Hospitals faced blood shortages in Ataq as medical teams responded to casualties and families searched for missing relatives.

The attack was followed by retaliatory strikes by government forces near Taiz, raising further concerns over the worsening humanitarian crisis in Yemen.

Reporting from the capital, Sanaa, Al Jazeera’s Yousef Mawry said, “The Houthis are not backing down. Their military spokesman says they are continuing to conduct more missile attacks deep inside Saudi Arabia.”

“As cross-border attacks grow, Yemenis fear the war is coming closer to home, especially as both sides threaten to escalate their attacks, while Saudi Arabia steps up its air campaign,” Mawry added.

Meanwhile, Yemen’s Saudi-backed coalition spokesperson Turki al-Maliki said on Tuesday that its forces have destroyed 127 Houthi weapons depots and missile launch platforms.
